rules: The output must be vertical 9:16 and visually upright, not sideways.
Audio must contain only real environmental and construction sounds. No music or cinematic audio is allowed.
The project must be built by exactly one worker only during the construction phase.

Never show heavy machinery or industrial construction equipment.

CRITICAL POV OPENING RULE: Scene 1 must be a strict first-person BODYCAM POV walking forward through a normal ordinary home interior toward a specific spot in the home. The camera IS the man's own eyes — we see only what he sees. The man whose POV this is must NEVER be visible: no body, no back, no shoulders, no head, no arms, no legs, no reflection. There must NEVER be a separate person seen walking ahead of, beside, or in front of the camera — this is never a third-person or over-the-shoulder follow shot.

CRITICAL POV REALISM — HANDHELD PHONE FEEL: The Scene 1 POV must look and feel like a real person physically holding a phone at chest or eye level while casually walking through their own home. It must NOT look like a cinematic camera, a gimbal, a drone, a Steadicam, a dolly, a video game walkthrough, or a real estate tour. Required imperfections: subtle handheld shake, tiny footstep bounce/bob, slight uneven pacing, small natural turns, occasional micro-adjustments as if the person is physically navigating around furniture and through doorways. The movement must NOT be perfectly smooth, perfectly centered, perfectly symmetrical, or cinematically composed. The camera should occasionally drift slightly off-center, correct itself, and show small realistic imperfections such as: slight bobbing from footsteps, tiny hand tremors, brief focus or exposure adjustments as lighting changes between rooms, small pauses before turning corners, minor overcorrections when approaching the hidden door, natural head and hand movement, imperfect framing, casual unhurried walking speed, and ordinary household lighting. This is one of only two scenes where handheld camera motion is allowed.

CRITICAL POV FORWARD PROGRESS: Scene 1 must depict the POV walking FROM the opening position (e.g. just inside the front door, entryway, top of hallway) TO the location of the secret entrance. By the END of Scene 1 (K1), the POV must have arrived directly in front of an ordinary, closed, full-size interior door — NO hand visible reaching for the handle and no hand touching the door. The door will open by itself in Scene 2. The start position (K0) and end position (K1) of Scene 1 must be in visibly different rooms or significantly different depths within the home, with different walls, different furniture, and different framing targets visible. K0 and K1 must never depict the same hallway, same wall, or same framing.

CRITICAL SCENE 1 END FRAME: Scene 1's end frame (K1) must show the bodycam POV arrived directly in front of an ordinary, closed, full-size door — NO hand reaching for the handle, NO hand touching the door, NO arm or fingers visible on the door at all. This is NOT just walking — K1 is the arrival at the door. The door stays closed in K1; the actual opening happens by itself in Scene 2. There is no hand, no button, and no motor.

CRITICAL LIVED-IN HOME ENVIRONMENT: The home shown in Scene 1 must feel ordinary, messy-but-real, and lived-in — like a normal family actually lives there. Include realistic everyday details such as: family shoes near the door, a laundry basket, kids' toys on the floor or shelf, mail or keys on a counter, jackets on hooks, garage clutter, basement storage bins, ordinary walls with scuff marks, normal overhead lighting or lamps, slightly cluttered countertops, a coat rack, pet bowls, backpacks, or similar suburban family details. The home must NOT look like a luxury showroom, a staged model home, a minimalist design magazine, or an empty pristine house. It should feel like a real dad's real house.

Scene 2 must show the ordinary door swinging open BY ITSELF on its hinges (no hand involved) and the bodycam POV then stepping forward through the open doorway into the dark or raw hidden space. Scene 2 begins with the closed door (continuing from K1) and ends with the POV inside the hidden room looking at the raw unfinished space, the open door visible to the side. No human hand appears on the door at any point in Scene 2.

CRITICAL TRANSITION RULE: After the secret entrance is fully opened and the hidden room is entered in Scene 2, ALL subsequent scenes must switch to a fully locked static camera. No more POV. No more handheld motion. The camera must be absolutely rock-steady with zero vibration, zero shake, zero jitter, and zero micro-movement, as if bolted to an immovable tripod inside the hidden room.

All construction scenes are construction timelapse scenes filmed from the same fixed static camera position inside the hidden room. The camera angle, framing, lens feel, and position must remain pixel-perfect identical across all construction scenes.

The hidden room location must remain locked from the moment of reveal. The same walls, ceiling, floor footprint, entrance position, and room dimensions must stay consistent across all construction scenes.

The construction must progress logically across scenes: starting with raw empty hidden space with bare walls, exposed studs, or unfinished surfaces, progressing through mid-build with framing, drywall, flooring, and rough utilities, then finishing stage with paint, wall treatments, lighting fixtures, and major furniture, and ending with fully finished hidden man cave reveal with all furnishings, lighting on, and clearly visible entrance.
The home must feel ordinary, suburban, and relatable. Avoid mansions, luxury estates, or impossibly large houses. The exterior context should be a normal family home.

The hidden room must be human-scale and believable for one worker. Room size should feel like a converted basement room, large closet expansion, or modest spare-room conversion, not a giant mansion lounge or impossible architecture.

CRITICAL ROOM SIZE CONSISTENCY: The hidden room's physical dimensions — width, depth, ceiling height, and overall footprint — must remain EXACTLY the same in every construction scene and the final reveal. The floor area must remain identical. No expansion, no widening, no deepening, no ceiling raising, no magical extra space appearing.
Every visible construction step must match realistic human labor capacity.

No floating objects, impossible engineering, magical appearance of structures, or unrealistic scale jumps.

The POV person's body must never be visible in Scene 1-2 keyframes — no hand, no arm, no fingers, no wrist on the door at any point (the door opens by itself). Never show a separate person walking ahead of, beside, or in front of the camera — this is strict bodycam POV.
Camera position must remain pixel-perfect consistent between construction keyframes with zero positional drift, zero vibration artifacts, and zero framing shift.
Every keyframe must be exactly ONE single photographic frame. Never generate multi-frame, multi-panel, storyboard, grid, triptych, split-view, or before-and-after compositions.

CRITICAL: No two consecutive construction keyframes may depict the same build stage. Construction must progress logically from raw room through framing, mid-build, finishing, to fully finished reveal.

CRITICAL ROOM SIZE LOCK: The hidden room's physical dimensions — width, depth, ceiling height, and floor area — must remain EXACTLY the same in every construction keyframe and the final reveal. The walls must be in the same positions relative to the camera. The ceiling must be at the same height. The floor area must be identical. The room must NEVER appear to grow, expand, widen, deepen, or gain additional space. Compare each construction keyframe to the previous one: the room shell (wall positions, ceiling height, floor boundaries) must be identical. Only the materials, finishes, fixtures, and furnishings within the room change.

CRITICAL POV vs CONSTRUCTION VISUAL STYLE: Scene 1-2 keyframes (POV phase) should look like frames from raw handheld phone footage — slightly imperfect framing, natural uneven lighting, casual composition. Construction keyframes (Scene 3+) should look like frames from a locked static tripod — perfectly stable, consistent framing, professional documentation angle. These two visual styles must be clearly distinct.

CRITICAL K1→K2 DOOR CONTINUITY: The ordinary closed door shown in K1 (hand on the handle) must be the SAME door shown open in K2. The door frame material, wall color/texture, flooring at the threshold, and door geometry must be consistent between K1 and K2. The door must NOT change appearance, type, size, or position. K2 must feel like the natural continuation of K1 — the man pushed the same door open by hand and stepped through the same doorway.

CRITICAL DOOR PHYSICAL CONSISTENCY: The ordinary door must be the EXACT SAME door across K1 and K2. The planner MUST describe the door using IDENTICAL specific details in BOTH end_keyframe_prompts — same door TYPE (e.g. plain closet door / basement door / utility-room door), same COLOR, same MATERIAL/wood grain/paint finish, same HANDLE shape and color, same HINGE style, same DIMENSIONS. Use the same descriptive phrase for the door in K1 and K2 so the video generator cannot drift. The door MUST NOT morph, change type, change color, change material, change handle, or change between a panel/closet/basement/etc. door between K1 and K2 or during the Scene 2 video clip. In K1 the door is closed with a hand on the handle; in K2 the SAME door is open after being pushed by hand. The door must look like the same solid object in both frames — never a sliding panel, never motorized, never vanishing.

CRITICAL WALL FINISH LOCK: Once any wall finish (paint color, stain, wallpaper, paneling) is applied in a construction keyframe, that EXACT color, tone, and finish must remain unchanged in every subsequent construction keyframe and the final reveal. Walls must NOT be repainted, change color, change tone, or vary in appearance once a finish has been applied. Pin the specific color (e.g. 'warm grey #888', 'deep navy', 'matte off-white') in the keyframe where it first appears and reuse the IDENTICAL color description in every later keyframe. The same lock applies to ceiling and floor finishes.
composition_rules: The image must be vertical portrait 9:16 composition.

CRITICAL: The output must be exactly ONE single continuous photographic frame. Never generate multiple frames, panels, sub-images, split views, storyboard grids, comic-strip layouts, triptychs, before-and-after comparisons, side-by-side views, or any multi-frame composition within a single image.

Scene 1 keyframe (K1) uses first-person bodycam POV composition at natural human eye level, showing the man arrived in front of an ordinary, closed, full-size door — NO hand visible reaching for, touching, or gripping the handle or any part of the door. The door is closed and the POV is simply standing at it. The door is a normal hinged door with visible thickness (1-2 inches of edge profile), realistic material texture, and a real handle. No floating button and no device disconnected from a surface. The framing should be slightly imperfect and casual — like a frame from raw bodycam/phone footage, NOT a perfectly composed cinematic shot. Slightly off-center framing is acceptable and encouraged.

Scene 2 keyframe (K2) uses first-person bodycam POV composition inside the hidden room, looking at the raw unfinished space. The same ordinary door, now pushed open on its hinges, must be partially visible at the edge of frame or behind the camera position, confirming spatial continuity with K1. The open door must still show visible thickness and solid material.
Construction scenes use the same fixed static wide-angle composition inside the hidden room. The camera must show most of the room including the secret entrance.
The construction composition must include the secret entrance visible in the frame for every interior keyframe.
Use the same camera height, same tripod placement, same angle, same lens feel, same horizon line, and same framing across all construction scenes with zero variation and zero positional drift.

CRITICAL ROOM SIZE IN FRAME: The room's walls, ceiling, and floor must occupy the same proportions of the frame in every construction keyframe. If the left wall is at 15% from the left edge of frame in one keyframe, it must be at 15% in every subsequent keyframe. If the ceiling is at 20% from the top, it must stay at 20%. The room boundaries must not shift, expand, or contract within the frame composition.
Stage each construction scene so room-wide progress is obvious across walls, ceiling, floor, fixtures, and furnishings, not only through one small local object.
The hidden room should feel like a believable home renovation — human-scale, real residential dimensions, not a tiny closet and not a giant mansion lounge.
Background and surrounding home context should not bleed unnaturally into the hidden room. Only the secret entrance should be the visible connection.
Do not create split shots, collages, or multi-panel compositions.
